I. 
INTRODUCTION 
This case involves the Vermont Public Utility Commission’s (“Commission”) 
investigation into Vermont Gas Systems, Inc.’s (“VGS”) tariff filing requesting a 1.95% increase 
for non-gas rates (daily access and distribution charges) and a $4.44 million withdrawal from the 
System Expansion and Reliability Fund (“SERF”).1  The resulting overall rate increase of 2.6% 
is based on forecasted gas costs. 
In today’s Order, the Commission determines that VGS’s proposed 1.95% increase for 
non-gas costs should be approved effective for bills rendered on or after November 1, 2021.  
Over the course of this proceeding, the Vermont Department of Public Service (“Department”)

trajectory that would otherwise have been expected to result from VGS’s Addison Natural Gas Project.

identified 11 areas of disagreement related to VGS’s cost of service as well as whether VGS 
should be required to use more SERF funds.  In the first section under the Findings and 
Discussion portion of this Order, we address why it is appropriate for VGS to withdraw SERF 
funds that result in a 1.95% increase to non-gas rates.  In that section, we also address the areas 
of agreement between VGS and the Department.  In subsequent sections, we address each of the 
remaining areas of disagreement between VGS and the Department regarding the cost of service.   
As described below, the Commission finds in favor of VGS on some cost-of-service 
items and in favor of the Department on other items.  We require VGS to recalculate the cost of 
service based on the Commission’s decisions in the areas of disagreement and then calculate the 
amount of SERF withdrawal that will result in a 1.95% increase to non-gas costs.  Accordingly, 
we also require VGS to make a compliance filing in this case documenting the final SERF 
withdrawal amount based on the Commission’s determinations on the cost-of-service items 
discussed below.  We also condition our approval on VGS providing notice to the Commission 
and Department regarding training availability for local fire departments and on VGS tracking 
certain costs related to transmission pipeline maintenance expenses.   
II. 
PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
On February 16, 2021, VGS filed a petition requesting a 1.95% increase in firm non-gas 
rates to be effective November 1, 2021.  VGS also requested that the Commission suspend the 
effectiveness of the proposed tariffs pursuant to Section 226(a) with implementation occurring 
on November 1, 2021, after the conclusion of the Section 227(a) seven-month review period.  
VGS also requested use of $4.44 million of the SERF to reduce the cost of service. 
On March 29, 2021, the Commission suspended the effectiveness of the proposed tariffs, 
opened this investigation into the proposed rate change, and set a schedule for the proceeding. 
No motions to intervene were filed.  There were no public comments filed in this 
proceeding. 
Over the course of this proceeding, the Department served three rounds of discovery on 
VGS.  The Department submitted direct testimony on June 10, 2021, and surrebuttal testimony 
on August 11, 2021.

  VGS served two rounds of discovery on the Department.  On July 9, 2021, VGS filed 
rebuttal testimony and revised its original proposal to reflect a reduction to its cost of service. 
VGS requested to reduce its SERF withdrawal to $4.14 million while maintaining its request for 
a 1.95% increase to non-gas costs. 
On August 11, 2021, the Department filed surrebuttal testimony requesting that the 
Commission authorize a 1.41% increase to VGS’s non-gas costs based on 11 areas of 
disagreement that would result in a reduction to VGS’s cost of service.  The Department 
recommends using $3.785 million of the SERF and requests that the Commission increase the 
amount of SERF funds utilized in the event that any of the areas of disagreement are decided in 
favor of VGS. 
On August 26 and 27, 2021, the Commission held an evidentiary hearing in this case.  At 
the evidentiary hearing, the testimony and exhibits listed in Joint Exhibit-1 were admitted into 
the evidentiary record as well as cross exhibits.   
On September 15, 2021, the parties filed their post-hearing briefs and proposed findings 
of fact. 
On September 22, 2021, the parties filed reply briefs. 
III. 
LEGAL STANDARDS 
Traditional rate cases filed pursuant to 30 V.S.A. § 225 are subject to the “just and 
reasonable” standard.2  The Vermont Supreme Court explained the process for determining just 
and reasonable rates as follows: 
The [Commission] seeks to establish utility rates for the immediate future that will 
allow investors a reasonable return without overcharging the ratepayers. As the first 
step in arriving at a fair rate of return, the [Commission] determines the operating 
expenses and the “rate base”—the utility’s net plant investment—for the “test 
year,” usually the most recent full calendar year . . . .  The [Commission] then 
adjusts the rate base by modifying the test year rate base to reflect “known and 
measurable” changes in plant investment. These are changes that are measurable 
with a reasonable degree of accuracy and have a high probability of being in effect 
in the adjusted test year . . . .  Finally, the [Commission] calculates an appropriate 
return on the adjusted rate base and devises adjusted rates that will produce a fair 
 
2 See Petition of Village of Hardwick Elec. Dept., 143 Vt. 437, 466 A.2d 1180 (1983) (“By statute, the 
[Commission] is required to set rates that are just and reasonable.”).

Case No. 21-0898-TF 
 
Page 5 
 
 
rate of return on the company's property in the immediate future.3  
 
Adjustments for operating expenses and capital investments are generally subject to the “known 
and measurable” standard, which allows changes that are “measurable with a reasonable degree 
of accuracy and have a high probability of being in effect in the adjusted test year.”4  In 
traditional rate proceedings, it is the utility’s responsibility to satisfy this standard: “the burden of 
supporting [a] change in rates or rate structure [rests] squarely on the proponent utility.”5 
In Bluefield Waterworks v. Public Service Commission, the United States Supreme Court 
set certain constitutional limitations that guide Commission review of a traditional rate 
proceeding.  Specifically, the Bluefield Court held: 
A public utility is entitled to such rates as will permit it to earn a return on the value 
of the property which it employs for the convenience of the public equal to that 
generally being made at the same time and in the same general part of the country 
on investments in other business undertakings which are attended by corresponding 
risks and uncertainties; but it has no constitutional right to profits such as are 
realized or anticipated in highly profitable enterprises or speculative ventures. The 
return should be reasonably sufficient to assure confidence in the financial 
soundness of the utility and should be adequate, under efficient and economical 
management, to maintain and support its credit and enable it to raise the money 
necessary for the proper discharge of its public duties.6 
 
The Vermont Supreme Court, in interpreting Bluefield, opined that “[r]ates cannot be set 
so low as to be confiscatory for the utility nor so high as to be excessive for the consumer . . . . 
Between these extremes lies a ‘zone of reasonableness’ within which a regulatory commission is 
free to set rates without judicial intervention.”7  In prior decisions, we have recognized that “it is 
the ‘substance and effect’ of the [Commission’s] actions which must bear judicial scrutiny.  The

4 Central Vermont Public Service Co., Dockets 6946 & 6988, Order of 3/29/05, at 67. 
5 In re Consolidated Rate Appeals of Green Mountain Power Co., 142 Vt. 373, 381, 455 A.2d 823, 826 (1983); 
see also In re Green Mountain Power Co., 162 Vt. at 386, 648 A.2d at 379. 
6 Bluefield Water Works & Improvement Co. v. Public Service Commission, 262 U.S. 679, 692–93 (1923). 
7 Petition of Village of Hardwick Elec. Dept., 143 Vt. at 44, 466 A.2d at 1183 (citing In re New England 
Telephone & Telegraph Co., 139 Vt. 578, 586, 433 A.2d 263, 267–68 (1981); Permian Basin Area Rate Cases, 390 
U.S. 747, 767, 88 S.Ct. 1344, 1360, 20 L.Ed.2d 312 (1968); In re New England Telephone & Telegraph Co., 139 Vt. 
578, 586, 433 A.2d 263, 267–68 (1981)).

United States Supreme Court has taken the same view of utility regulation by establishing that it 
is the ‘end result’ which must meet the constitutional test.”8 
Under Bluefield, a utility does not hold a right of return, but is instead entitled to a “fair 
opportunity to earn a reasonable rate of return.”9  Moreover, longstanding Vermont law 
authorizes “the Commission to consider management efficiency and customer service in arriving 
at a determination of just and reasonable rates.”10  Thus, we follow the above legal standards set 
by the United States Supreme Court, the Vermont Supreme Court, and the Commission in 
deciding this case. 
IV. 
FINDINGS 
A. 
SERF, Return on Equity, and Undisputed Cost of Service Adjustments  
1. This case addresses the non-gas rate components of VGS’s cost of service.  These 
components are the daily access and distribution charges and are collectively identified as the 
“Base Rate.”  The natural gas charge component of VGS’s rates is modified on a quarterly basis 
pursuant to the purchase gas adjustment approved in Case No. 19-3529-PET as part of VGS’s 
alternative regulation plan.  Andrea McNeil, VGS (“McNeil”) pf. at 3. 
2. The test year is the 12-month period ending December 31, 2020, and the rate year is 
the 12-month period from October 1, 2021, through September 30, 2022.  McNeil pf. at 8. 
3. VGS initially proposed a non-gas rate increase of 1.95% and utilization of $4.4 
million from the SERF.  Exh.VGS-MM-1. 
4. The Department initially recommended reducing VGS’s proposed non-gas revenue 
requirement by $1.1 million and using $4.3 million from the SERF.  Scott Wheeler, Department 
(“Wheeler”) pf. at 2. 
5. In last year’s rate case, Case No. 20-0431-TF, VGS initially sought a 3% increase to 
non-gas rates and utilization of $5.58 million of the SERF.  VGS revised its request by reducing 
its proposed ROE, reducing its short-term interest rates, and cutting $225,000 in operating

SERF 
6. The SERF was approved by the Commission in 2011 in Docket No. 7712 to mitigate 
future rate increases associated with VGS’s expansion into Addison County.  The intended result 
is to return SERF funds to customers over time while ensuring that customers benefit from the 
rate-smoothing effect of utilizing the SERF in a measured and strategic manner.  McNeil pf. at 7. 
7. Under its initial rate proposal in this case, VGS’s residential customers would be 
paying on average $260 less per year than they were paying in November 2011 (in nominal 
dollars).  McNeil pf. at 5. 
8. Utilizing $1 million in SERF funds in a given rate year enables VGS to avoid a 
roughly 2% change in non-gas rates for its customers.  For example, if VGS reduced its initial 
SERF utilization in this case by $1 million (from $4.44 million to $3.44 million), the resulting 
effect on non-gas rates would increase from the 1.95% VGS requested to 3.80%.  McNeil pf. at 
7. 
9. On the other hand, if VGS were to maintain SERF withdrawals at $5.58 million (the 
level used in the previous rate case), there would be no change in non-gas rates in this rate year, 
but the difference would be pushed to future years.  McNeil pf. at 7. 
10. The use of $4 million of SERF funds in this case suggests that VGS is avoiding an 
approximately 8% increase to non-gas rate in the next year.  Assuming no additional changes to 
the cost of service in the next two years, VGS is looking at a 4% base rate increase in each of the 
next two rate years if no SERF funds are utilized.  Tr. 8/26/21, vol. I, at 64 (McNeil). 
11. If VGS returns approximately $4 million in SERF funds to customers in this case, it 
will have approximately $3.9 million remaining to utilize in the next two years.  Tr. 8/26/21, vol. 
I, at 66 (McNeil).

enough available SERF funds to help smooth rate pressure in the next two years.  Tr. 8/26/21,

Return on Equity 
13. In this case, VGS proposed a return on equity (“ROE”) of 8.8%.  The proposed ROE 
is based on the approved ROE of 8.65% in Case No. 20-0413-TF adjusted by one-half the 
change in the composite 10-Year Treasury Note Rate.  Matthew Mitchell, VGS (“Mitchell”) pf. 
at 18. 
14. The Department calculated the cost of equity by applying a constant growth 
discounted cash flow (“DCF”) model and a capital asset pricing model (“CAPM”) to a group of 
proxy companies and by performing a risk premium (“RP”) analysis using the previously 
authorized ROE.  Zhen Zhu, Department (“Zhu”) pf. at 3-4. 
15. The Department’s calculations indicate that VGS’s required cost of equity, or the 
opportunity cost of equity, is 8.49% based on the median value of ROE resulting from the DCF, 
CAPM, and RP models.  The average ROE from the three models is 8.60%, and the midpoint of 
ROE is 8.74%.  Even though the 8.8% requested ROE is higher than the market-value-based 
ROE, the Department finds 8.8% to be “generally reasonable and acceptable.”  Zhu pf. at 5, 45.

Discussion 
The SERF was created to reserve funds associated with a decrease in gas costs to smooth 
rates for VGS’s customers in future years.  VGS would then be able to phase in the financial 
effects of the extension of its transmission pipeline into Addison County.  Since the SERF was 
created, VGS has used the funds to offset increases to its cost of service.  Therefore, SERF 
withdrawals result in a lower increase to non-gas rates in any given year than otherwise would be 
needed.  With less than $8 million left in the SERF, the Commission sees value in spreading the 
withdrawal of these remaining funds over the next few years to avoid rate shock in any given 
year.  If the Commission were to authorize a higher withdrawal from the SERF to offset rates 
this year, VGS testified that larger rate increases would likely be required in the subsequent two 
to three years as the SERF is depleted.   
In its testimony of August 11, the Department recommends several downward 
adjustments to the cost of service totaling $654,06811 and a lower top-line number for the 
increase to base rates of 1.41%.   On their own, these downward adjustments would result in a 
lower SERF withdrawal.  However, the Department still advocates a top-line 1.41% increase to 
base rates.12  Below, we rule on each of the remaining disputed cost-of-service items, which 
changes the underlying calculation of how much SERF must be used to achieve a 1.41% increase 
in base rates.  Given that the cost of service will not be reduced by the full amount recommended 
by the Department, SERF withdrawals would need to be larger to allow for the lower rate 
increase of 1.41%.  However, if the Commission allows VGS’s proposed rate increase of 1.95% 
to go into effect, more funds will remain in the SERF to smooth rates for customers over the next 
few years. 
With that in mind, the Commission approves VGS’s proposed top-line 1.95% increase in 
base rates this year.  In this Order, we also rule on each of the Department’s recommended

Discussion 
 
The Department argues that VGS should be required to reduce its outside legal-services 
expenses for rate proceedings and regulatory matters by $80,227.  “Given that VGS’s internal 
regulatory counsel is tasked with all work related to regulatory matters as well as work related to 
VGS’s participation in rate proceedings, it would be unjust and unreasonable to charge 
customers twice for this work.”13 
 
 
VGS argues that the Commission should adopt its three-year average without the 
Department’s reductions for two reasons.  First, VGS contends that its three-year average is 
conservative due to the abnormally low expenses in 2020 resulting from the pandemic, which 
brought the average down.14  Second, VGS opposes the Department’s reduction as not known 
and measurable or based on evidence before the Commission.15  VGS defends its assessment that 
hiring an in-house regulatory counsel will not reduce outside legal expenses because outside 
counsel will continue to be hired for rate cases and other regulatory matters and the in-house 
counsel job description mostly consists of internal tasks.16 
 
We adopt VGS’s three-year average for outside legal expenses without the Department’s 
reduction.  We agree with VGS that the three-year average factors in the abnormally low outside 
legal expenses for 2020 and is an appropriate estimate of outside legal expenses for the rate year.  
Further, we do not have evidence in the case to support the Department’s contention that 
regulatory counsel will reduce the workload for outside legal counsel because VGS has not 
provided detailed testimony explaining the roles for each legal representative in a situation where 
the job descriptions appear to overlap.  While we certainly agree with the Department that VGS 
will not recover twice for the same expense, we do not understand the employment of an in-
house regulatory counsel to create double recovery.  In a future rate case, we will better

Discussion 
 
The Department argues that $38,475 should be removed from the cost of service because 
these costs are community goodwill endeavors that do not benefit ratepayers.18  The Department 
sets out the 25 expenses that it contends should be removed and provides justifications for each 
expense.19  The Department asserts that it would be unjust and unreasonable to expect ratepayers 
to pay for these expenditures.20   
 
VGS agrees to a $6,425 downward adjustment to remove certain costs that may not be 
recoverable.21  The costs identified for exclusion from the advertising account include local

Furthermore, under Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Accounting Release 12 
(“FERC AR-12”), “expenditures made by the utility resulting from employment practices that 
were found to be discriminatory by judicial or administrative decree, or that were the result of a 
compromise settlement or consent decree are to be reported in Account 426” and excluded from 
the cost of service.28  In applying the principles of FERC AR-12, the DC Public Service 
Commission stated that “any expenditures . . . related to employment . . . discrimination cases 
terminated by compromise settlement or consent decree are presumptively unjust, unreasonable, 
and discriminatory, and are, therefore presumptively unlawful.”29  This creates a rebuttable 
presumption that expenses associated with discrimination claims should be booked into Account 
426 and excluded from rates.  The Vermont Public Utility Commission has yet to rule on such a 
case but nonetheless adopts the principles of FERC AR-12.  
 
In the present case, we exclude the settlement and associated costs from the cost of 
service on the basis that they are unlikely to recur in the rate year, so we do not reach the 
question of whether the specific costs related to the 2020 settlement are presumptively unlawful 
and therefore whether ratepayers should bear the costs of that specific settlement.

Distribution Integrity Maintenance (Cross-Bore Expenses) 
63. The distribution maintenance expense at issue in this case concerns the appropriate 
amount to include in the cost of service for VGS’s legacy cross-bore program.  John St. Hilaire, 
VGS (“St. Hilaire”) pf. at 5. 
64. A “cross-bore” occurs when a natural gas line traverses through or “bores” a sewer 
line during the installation of the natural gas line.  This is a risk that has emerged more widely in 
the natural gas industry as “trenchless” installation technology has become more prevalent.  St. 
Hilaire pf. at 6. 
65. In 2020, VGS developed a program to address potential “legacy” cross-bores that 
occurred during previous system development.  In 2020, approximately $386,000 was included 
in the cost of service for VGS’s legacy cross-bore program.  St. Hilaire pf. at 6. 
66. In the present case, VGS continues the legacy cross-bore program at this level, 
escalated by $7,720 for an approximate inflationary adjustment.  St. Hilaire pf. at 6; exh. VGS-
MM-1, Schedule 4.  
67. The Department recommends that VGS reduce its spending on cross-bore inspections 
because it is outperforming its cross-bore program goals.  The Department is concerned that the 
current rapid pace of cross-bore inspection exceeds the baseline performance measure of 
inspections in 2019 and 2020 as specified in VGS’s distribution integrity management plan.  
Hunt pf. surreb. at 12. 
68. The cross-bore program was budgeted to be a 50-year program to assess 50,100 
laterals.  The number of inspections achieved in a given year is dependent on the area where the 
inspection is occurring.  Inspections in more densely populated areas result in more mains and

laterals being inspected per dollar spent.  Conversely, when the laterals are farther apart, the cost 
per lateral is higher.  Tr. 8/26/21, vol.I, at 75-76 (McNeil). 
69. Recent inspections have occurred in densely populated areas like Burlington where 
the cost per lateral inspection is lower, resulting in more inspections under the VGS budget than 
can be expected in later years.  Tr. 8/26/21, vol.I, at 75-76 (McNeil). 
 
Discussion 
The disagreement regarding VGS’s distribution integrity management expense turns on 
whether VGS plans to perform too many inspections in the rate year relative to the long-term 
distribution integrity management plan and whether that overperformance is just and reasonable.  
The distribution integrity management plan aims to inspect just over 50,000 laterals over the 
course of 50 years.  One might assume this means that VGS intends to inspect 1,000 laterals in 
any given year.  This assumption is not correct.  VGS is likely to perform more than 1,000 
inspections per year in the early years of the plan as it works in densely populated areas and 
fewer than 1,000 inspections in later years of the plan when it moves to less dense areas. 
Given that recent inspections have occurred in densely populated areas, VGS is not 
outperforming its distribution management plan.  The relatively high number of inspections 
performed in the most recent two years reflects the density of the areas where VGS has been 
inspecting lines, primarily in the Burlington area.  In the future, we expect that the number of 
lines inspected will slow as VGS begins inspections in less densely populated rural areas.   
Furthermore, if the Commission were to reduce the cost of service in this area, VGS 
would likely perform fewer cross-bore inspections.  Identifying and remediating cross-bores 
remains a high safety priority for the Commission, and we encourage VGS to continue its current 
pace of inspections.  We authorize the full amount requested by VGS in the cost of service for 
distribution integrity management, $770,688.
